tasks.title: AUSTRALIA’S SOCIAL MEDIA BAN
body: {{0}} There are an estimated 440,000 young Australian teens on Snapchat. On Instagram, 350,000 of that age group are active users, and on TikTok, 200,000. On December 10th, 2025, those numbers drastically changed under a landmark law that requires users in Australia to be at least 16 to have accounts on social media services.

{{1}} The platforms currently affected by the law are Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Reddit, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube. Other services widely used by young teens were excluded, because Australia’s eSafety commissioner deemed them to be primarily for messaging or gaming.

{{2}} The burden is on the tech companies to deactivate younger users by utilizing age estimation and verification technologies in addition to the user’s self-reported age. Regulators have said the companies may rely on factors like how long the account has been active, whether it interacts with other underage users, or facial or voice analysis.

{{3}} Tech companies have criticized the law as being rushed and poorly designed, saying teens will no longer benefit from features they have been introducing to make their platforms a safer place, like parental controls. Most have said they still intend to comply with the law.

{{4}} There are no punishments for children or parents who continue to access social media after the law takes effect. The companies, however, can face fines of up to 50 million Australian dollars for not taking reasonable steps to prevent users younger than 16 from having accounts on their platforms.

{{5}} In promoting the law, Australian officials have highlighted concerns about social media being a vehicle for online bullying, an amplifier of anxiety, a conduit of peer pressure and a tool for potential predators.

{{6}} In a large-scale survey of 9- to 16-year-olds by the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, the nation’s public broadcaster, the vast majority of teens said that they did not think the ban would work. Three-quarters of all of the children polled said they planned on continuing to use social media.

tasks.title: THE DANGERS OF LETTING AI PLAN YOUR NEXT TRIP
body: In just a few years, artificial intelligence (AI) tools like ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini have gone from a mere novelty to an integral part of trip planning for millions of people. 30% of travellers are now using AI tools and dedicated travel AI sites to help organise their trips.

While these programs can offer valuable travel tips, they can also lead people into some frustrating or even dangerous situations by providing incorrect information or steering them to a place that was created by the hard-wired imagination of a robot. A 2024 BBC article reported that AI trip planner Layla told users that there was an Eiffel Tower in Beijing and suggested a marathon route across Northern Italy that was entirely unfeasible. According to a 2024 survey, 37% of those who used AI to help plan their travels reported that it could not provide enough information, while around 33% complained their AI-generated recommendations included false information.

These issues stem from how AI generates its answers. According to Rayid Ghani, a professor in machine learning, large language models like ChatGPT work by analysing massive collections of text and putting together words and phrases that, statistically, feel like appropriate responses. Sometimes this provides perfectly accurate information, other times, you get what AI experts call a “hallucination”. However, it's often difficult for users to distinguish between the two. Recently, a young couple made the trek to a scenic cable car in Malaysia that they had seen on TikTok, only to find that no such structure existed. The video they'd watched had been entirely AI generated.

Currently, authorities are attempting to regulate how AI presents information to users, e.g. by including watermarks or other distinguishing features so viewers know when something has been altered or generated by AI. If these kinds of regulations do pass, they could make it easier for travellers to detect AI-generated images or videos.

One thing Ghani suggests is to be as specific as possible in your queries and verify absolutely everything. If an AI tool gives you a travel suggestion that sounds a little too perfect, double check it. Ironically, the time spent verifying AI information can easily make the process just as laborious as planning your trip the old-fashioned way.

tasks.title: WHY HUMANS ENJOY A GOOD FEAST TOGETHER
body: For thousands of years, humans have come together in small groups to feast on food. {{0}} We like to sit down together for a good tuck-in. Meals out with friends, dinner parties, holiday get-togethers where we regularly overindulge are all events we can relate to. {{24}} Sharing food as a behaviour is likely to go back to before the origin of our species. But giving food to those closest to you is not the same as having a meal together. Chimpanzees and bonobos, two of our closest primate relatives, also share food with their social groups. Humans seem to have added a number of complex social layers to this act.

{{25}} But no one is certain exactly when they first learned to cook. {{26}} But when someone has gone to the trouble of hunting or gathering food, putting together a fire, and then cooking over it, it implies that they may have a social group to help them with the many stages of this process. {{27}} As Robin Dunbar, an anthropologist at the University of Oxford found, those extra hours may have been golden opportunities for social bonding over food.

Whatever the details of its origins, eating meals together is linked to higher wellbeing, Dunbar found in a 2017 study that asked people living in the UK how often they ate meals with others. {{28}} “Eating triggers the brain's endorphin system, which is responsible for bonding between primates and humans,” Dunbar says. Eating together as a group enhances the endorphin effect in the same way that jogging together does. {{29}}

body: Few dishes better capture the story of Britain’s relationship with “foreign” food {{0}} chicken tikka masala. Its roots {{10}} northern India, where pieces of chicken were marinated in yoghurt, spices and acid, {{11}} cooked in a fiery oven. Served as dry tikka, it had a strong, smoky and spicy taste. But when Indian and South Asian chefs began opening restaurants in postwar Britain, they found people preferred mild dishes with sauce {{12}} very spicy or strong flavours. {{13}} began the slow alchemy that turned tikka into tikka masala – the chicken in sauce – a bridge between two gastronomic worlds.

Legend {{14}} its birth to a Glasgow curry house in the 1970s, where a dissatisfied customer found his chicken tikka too dry. The chef responded {{15}} mixing a tin of tomato soup, cream and spices, and ladling it over the meat. The trick worked: the dish quickly became a bestseller. In that moment, a recipe – or perhaps a myth – was born.
